questions.title: What evidence must an agency provide to prove a record was compiled for law enforcement purposes under FOIA Exemption 7(A)?
questions.question_body: In the Foad Farahi v. FBI case, the court said the FBI had to show that Farahi's file was compiled in furtherance of investigations of violations of national security and international terrorism to include pending law enforcement proceedings and the subject's association with individuals directly involved in such violations. I am unsure what kind of evidence is required to satisfy the compiled for law enforcement purposes part of Exemption 7(A). Does the agency need to show a direct nexus to a specific enforcement action, or is a general statement of investigative intent enough? What standards do courts use to evaluate this claim?

questions.title: How is pending or reasonably anticipated enforcement proceedings determined for FOIA Exemption 7(A) when an investigation has been open for years?
questions.question_body: The court highlighted that the FBI’s Bender declaration confirmed that the investigations remain ongoing as of March 2023, but Farahi argued that the passage of time undermines the claim of pending or reasonably anticipated enforcement proceedings. How do courts apply the standard over such a long period? Is a mere statement of ongoing sufficient, or must the agency demonstrate a realistic expectation that a proceeding will be taken within a specified time? What case law informs this analysis?

questions.title: What level of judicial deference is applied to the FBI’s Exemption 7(A) determinations in national-security FOIA cases?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that the government's determination is entitled to deference, especially in national-security contexts. But how is that deference quantified? Are there any limits or optional standards, such as deference only if the determination is reasonable or non-arbitrary? How do cases like Campbell v. DOJ, CNSS v. DOJ, and others guide the court's deference? When can a court override such a determination?

questions.title: What qualifies as a properly distinct category of documents for FOIA Exemption 7(A), and how do courts prevent overbroad categorization?
questions.question_body: The court noted that categories must be sufficiently distinct to allow a court to determine whether the claimed exemption applies to each category. In the Farahi case, the FBI used several categories but lacked detail. How do courts decide whether a category is overbroad? What criteria must the agency provide to justify the use of a category rather than itemizing documents? Is a brief description enough or does it require more specific information?

questions.title: What are the consequences of an FBI’s failure to meet the statutory FOIA response deadline?
questions.question_body: The office missed the statutory deadline and the plaintiff sued. In my understanding, FOIA requires agencies to respond within 3 months (extendable to 6 if needed). What remedies are available to plaintiffs when this deadline is missed? Does the failure automatically constitute a violation, or must the plaintiff file a complaint? How does the court treat such delays regarding summary judgment motions?

questions.title: Why does a court review a FOIA summary‑judgment grant de novo, and what does that mean for the parties?
questions.question_body: The court reviews a FOIA summary-judgment grant de novo. How does this differ from ordinary appellate review? What evidence can the moving party present, and what burden does the respondent carry? Why is the standard higher or lower for FOIA judgments, and what specific FOIA provisions influence this approach?

questions.title: When are ex parte FOIA affidavits allowed, and how do courts evaluate them against public affidavits?
questions.question_body: What rules govern the allowance of ex parte affidavits in FOIA cases? How do courts assess their reliability, especially when no counterpart is available? In the Farahi case, ex parte affidavits were pivotal; what precedent supports their use and what limitations exist?

questions.title: What does FOIA require of agencies to reasonably segregate and release nonexempt information when exempt and nonexempt text are interwoven?
questions.question_body: The faraha case involved ten thousand pages with potentially interspersed nonexempt words. The court found no reasonable segregation was possible. How do courts decide whether segregation is feasible? Are there specific tests or thresholds? What does past precedent (Mead Data Cent. v. US Dep't of Air Force, Perioperative Servs. v. US Dep't of Veterans Affs.) say about line-by-line redaction versus block segregation? When can a court demand a more detailed partial release?
